The university should show crowding forecasts as ranges, such as low, medium, or high, rather than as guaranteed numbers. This would help students choose quieter spaces while reminding them that the forecast itself may change behavior. If everyone sees that one floor will be crowded, many students may move elsewhere and create new congestion. The system should therefore update forecasts after major shifts and compare predictions with actual use. Presenting the information as conditional would preserve its practical value without suggesting false precision. Students could still use the forecast, but they would understand that their responses become part of the system being predicted.

Design B is better because the summary can guide attention without replacing information that may matter. A short summary could place the deadline and required action first, helping students who would otherwise ignore a long notice. However, an AI system may omit a rare exception. For example, a scholarship email might have a different deadline for international students. Keeping the original notice immediately below the summary allows those students to verify the condition before acting. The university should also label the summary as incomplete. This design gains the convenience of compression while reducing the risk of treating a reduced representation as the whole message.

The university should first group the ten plans by meaningful criteria, such as cost, flexibility, and meal frequency, and show one typical option in each group. This reduces the number of comparisons students must make before they know which differences matter. A student who cares mainly about low cost could start with that group instead of comparing all ten plans. Students with less common needs should still be able to open a full list or filter by special conditions. The goal is not to remove choice, but to organize it so that uncertain first-year students can compare options without pretending that one plan is best for everyone.

Two conditions are essential. First, participation should be voluntary, and wearable data should be treated as a proxy rather than a direct measure of health. A sleep estimate, for example, may be affected by movement patterns or device fit even when the student feels exhausted. Second, advice should combine device data with another source of evidence, such as a student report or clinical consultation when necessary. The university should also explain uncertainty instead of presenting one number as a diagnosis. These safeguards matter because a measured signal can change for reasons unrelated to the condition it is supposed to represent.

The university should combine a common exam, a practical assignment, and a short explanation of the student's reasoning. The exam gives comparable evidence across students, while the assignment shows whether knowledge can be applied. The explanation can reveal understanding that a score alone may miss. For example, students might memorize facts well enough to raise test scores without becoming better at solving unfamiliar problems. Using several measures makes that strategy less effective because improvement must appear in different forms of evidence. No measure is complete, so the university should treat each one as evidence about learning rather than as the definition of learning itself.

System B offers the best balance. If both names are visible, as in system A, students may soften criticism to protect friendships or reputation. Full anonymity in system C removes that pressure, but it also weakens accountability because careless comments are difficult to trace. Under system B, students are anonymous to each other, so they can criticize a draft more freely, while the instructor can still identify a reviewer who writes an unsupported or hostile comment. The review form should also require one specific problem and one suggested revision. This design reduces social pressure without allowing anonymity to become an excuse for low-quality feedback.

Recordings should be available after class, but access should be paired with a weekly task that requires students to use the course regularly. This gives students flexibility when they are ill or need to review a difficult explanation without turning recordings into an excuse to postpone the whole course. For example, each week students could answer two short questions based on that week's lectures. If someone waits until the final week to watch everything, those deadlines would reveal the problem early. The policy should therefore treat recordings as a backup and review tool, while the recurring task keeps students connected to the pace of the class.

The project grade could be 70 percent group work and 30 percent individual evidence. The group score would reward the quality of the final product and the team's ability to coordinate, which are genuine goals of collaborative work. The individual score could come from a short oral explanation and a reflection describing each student's contribution. For example, two students might receive the same group score, but a student who cannot explain the method used in the project would lose individual points. This system preserves an incentive to cooperate while giving the instructor separate evidence of what each student actually contributed and learned.

The university should guarantee access to campus housing but not require every first-year student to live there. Instead, all first-year students should join a small orientation group that meets several times during the first semester. This supports social connection directly rather than using residence as a rough substitute for it. A commuter who lives with family could join the same group activities as students in dormitories without paying for unnecessary housing. Students with caregiving, financial, or accessibility constraints should also be allowed alternatives. The policy would preserve opportunities to build community while recognizing that the same living arrangement creates very different costs for different students.

The university should require one course outside a student's main field during the first two years and let students choose from a broad list. The purpose should be to practice a different way of asking questions, not simply to accumulate unrelated credits. For example, a science student might take ethics and examine how evidence, values, and social consequences interact. One course is enough to create that exposure without taking substantial time from specialized study. Departments should also approve several options that connect naturally with their own fields. This structure makes breadth a deliberate learning goal while leaving most of the curriculum available for depth.

Grade distributions should be published with the response context: the assessment method, major assignment types, class size, and an explanation that past grades are not a complete measure of course quality. Without that context, students may treat a high average as evidence that a course is easy or good. For example, a demanding seminar with strong students could show high grades for a very different reason. Publishing only the distribution would turn a proxy into the outcome itself. Adding course goals and grading methods would help students interpret what the numbers represent and what they leave out before using them to choose classes.

The central library should receive 24-hour access before gyms or ordinary classrooms because it supports a wider range of academic needs, including late study and work between irregular schedules. The service should continue only when overnight demand is high enough to justify staffing and security costs. For example, the university could keep one floor open, require student-ID entry, and review usage data each term. If very few students use the space, hours should be reduced rather than keeping the policy permanently. Prioritizing one central facility provides flexibility while avoiding the cost and security burden of opening many buildings throughout the night.

AI should be allowed when it supports a student's reasoning but not when it replaces the reasoning or writing being assessed. Asking a tool to suggest counterarguments or identify an unclear sentence is acceptable because the student still evaluates the ideas and produces the final argument. Submitting AI-generated paragraphs as original work should not be allowed when the assignment is meant to test writing ability. Students should briefly disclose what tool they used and for what purpose. Instructors could also ask for notes or a short oral explanation when authorship is uncertain. This boundary separates assistance from substitution by focusing on the skill the assignment is supposed to measure.

Attendance should affect grades only when being present is necessary to demonstrate the skill the course is assessing. In a laboratory, clinical exercise, or discussion class, participation produces evidence that cannot be replaced by reading notes later. A large lecture is different: if students can demonstrate the same knowledge on assignments and exams, attendance itself should not earn points. For example, missing a patient-interview practice session may justify losing participation credit, while missing a recorded lecture should not. Courses should also allow reasonable exceptions for illness or emergencies. The rule should measure required learning activity rather than punish absence as an end in itself.

Activities that mainly deliver information can move online, while activities whose value depends on immediate interaction should remain face to face. A large lecture explaining established concepts could be streamed because students can receive the same content without traveling to campus. A laboratory, clinical exercise, or small discussion should stay in person because students must respond to equipment or other people in real time. The university should therefore classify activities by what students must actually do, not by course title. This principle keeps the flexibility of online teaching while protecting forms of learning that lose important information or practice when moved to a screen.

The seminar should focus on evaluating and using evidence across fields. A sample task could ask students to read a short article, identify its main claim, and write a response that supports or challenges the claim with specific evidence. That skill transfers to science, humanities, and professional courses because students in all fields must distinguish claims from support. To avoid becoming extra general workload, the seminar should stay small and use examples chosen by each department. The requirement should assess one transferable process rather than cover many unrelated topics. This would give first-year students a common academic foundation while allowing the content to remain relevant to their field.

Students should see response rates, summary ratings for several dimensions, and recurring themes from written comments, but not raw comments that could identify individuals or give one extreme opinion too much weight. The page should also state that course evaluations measure student perceptions, not teaching quality directly. For example, a course with a low workload rating might still require difficult independent study. Showing only one average score could hide that difference. Summarizing several indicators and reporting how many students responded would make the evidence easier to interpret while reducing the chance that a small or unusual group is treated as representative of the whole class.

Students could choose between two preset weighting plans: 60 percent exams and 40 percent assignments, or 40 percent exams and 60 percent assignments. Everyone would still complete both forms of assessment, and the choice would have to be made before the first major score is returned. These rules preserve comparability because every student is judged on the same two skills within a limited range. Complete freedom would let students avoid whichever assessment exposes a weakness and would make final grades mean different things across students. A constrained choice provides flexibility without turning the grading system into a different course for each person.

The reflection should ask two questions: What caused your most important error, and what will you change before the next assessment? Students should receive credit for giving a specific explanation and a realistic next action, not for claiming that they worked hard or felt disappointed. For example, a student who lost points through rushed reading might plan to reserve five minutes for checking question wording next time. The task should be brief and worth only a small amount of credit. Grading specificity rather than self-praise would make the reflection useful for future improvement and reduce the incentive to write empty comments that simply sound responsible.

Students should be allowed to add or drop courses without penalty during the first two weeks, but after that point changes should require a documented reason. This gives students enough time to discover whether a course matches their preparation and workload. At the same time, a firm deadline prevents students from holding scarce seats while other students remain unable to enroll. For example, a student could try two overlapping electives during week one but would need to release one seat before week three. The rule protects useful exploration while limiting the scheduling and teaching costs created by unlimited late changes.

The university should display crowding as a range, such as low, medium, or high, together with the time of the latest update. Exact numbers may suggest more certainty than the estimate deserves, and the information itself can change where students go. For example, a library labeled very crowded may quickly become less crowded if many students choose another space. The system should therefore refresh frequently and avoid identifying individual users. It could also show several nearby alternatives instead of directing everyone to one location. This design would help students act on the information while reducing privacy risk, false precision, and crowding created by the forecast itself.

The requirement should apply only if the activity has a clear educational purpose and students can meet it through several approved routes. The goal should be to connect academic knowledge with real community problems, not simply to require unpaid service. For example, students might tutor schoolchildren, support a health survey, or analyze data for a nonprofit. The university should provide alternatives or exemptions for students whose paid work, caregiving, disability, or travel limits make a standard placement difficult. These conditions keep the requirement focused on learning while preventing one fixed activity from imposing very different costs on students with different circumstances.
